assignments.title: Graded Recitation: Speak the Poem
assignments.html:
Graded Recitation: Speak the Poem
English 3 · Module 3
20 pointsRecording, or live with your teacherEyes coveredDue in Week 6
Perform a Victorian-era poem from memory, with eyes covered: the whole poem you choose below, or its marked span.
What to do
 
1Choose one poem. Read all seven aloud once, then pick the one your voice returns to.
2Learn it by heart. Let the line breaks decide where you breathe, and the meter be a pulse, not a hammer. Let your voice mark the turn.
3Perform it. Wear a blindfold, close your eyes, or turn away from any page or screen. No reading.
Choose one poem (16 to 37 lines)
 
1
The Poor Orphan Child
Charlotte Brontë · the ballad Bessie sings, Jane Eyre, chapter 3 (1847) · Whole poem, 20 lines in five stanzas

My feet they are sore, and my limbs they are weary;
Long is the way, and the mountains are wild;
Soon will the twilight close moonless and dreary
Over the path of the poor orphan child.

Why did they send me so far and so lonely,
Up where the moors spread and grey rocks are piled?
Men are hard-hearted, and kind angels only
Watch o’er the steps of a poor orphan child.

Yet distant and soft the night breeze is blowing,
Clouds there are none, and clear stars beam mild,
God, in His mercy, protection is showing,
Comfort and hope to the poor orphan child.

Ev’n should I fall o’er the broken bridge passing,
Or stray in the marshes, by false lights beguiled,
Still will my Father, with promise and blessing,
Take to His bosom the poor orphan child.

There is a thought that for strength should avail me,
Though both of shelter and kindred despoiled;
Heaven is a home, and a rest will not fail me;
God is a friend to the poor orphan child.

POEM 1 · JANE EYRE, CHAPTER 3 (CHARLOTTE BRONTË, 1847)
2
A song sung in chapter 24
Charlotte Brontë · Jane Eyre, chapter 24 (1847) · The first six stanzas, 24 lines, from “The truest love that ever heart” to “Disasters gather nigh.”

The truest love that ever heart
Felt at its kindled core,
Did through each vein, in quickened start,
The tide of being pour.

Her coming was my hope each day,
Her parting was my pain;
The chance that did her steps delay
Was ice in every vein.

I dreamed it would be nameless bliss,
As I loved, loved to be;
And to this object did I press
As blind as eagerly.

But wide as pathless was the space
That lay our lives between,
And dangerous as the foamy race
Of ocean-surges green.

And haunted as a robber-path
Through wilderness or wood;
For Might and Right, and Woe and Wrath,
Between our spirits stood.

I dangers dared; I hindrance scorned;
I omens did defy:
Whatever menaced, harassed, warned,
I passed impetuous by.

POEM 2 · JANE EYRE, CHAPTER 24 (CHARLOTTE BRONTË, 1847)
3
“Life”
Charlotte Brontë · from Poems by Currer, Ellis, and Acton Bell (1846) · Whole poem, 24 lines

Life, believe, is not a dream
So dark as sages say;
Oft a little morning rain
Foretells a pleasant day.
Sometimes there are clouds of gloom,
But these are transient all;
If the shower will make the roses bloom,
O why lament its fall?
Rapidly, merrily,
Life’s sunny hours flit by,
Gratefully, cheerily
Enjoy them as they fly!
What though Death at times steps in,
And calls our Best away?
What though sorrow seems to win,
O’er hope, a heavy sway?
Yet Hope again elastic springs,
Unconquered, though she fell;
Still buoyant are her golden wings,
Still strong to bear us well.
Manfully, fearlessly,
The day of trial bear,
For gloriously, victoriously,
Can courage quell despair!

POEM 3 · POEMS BY CURRER, ELLIS, AND ACTON BELL (1846)
4
“No Coward Soul Is Mine”
Emily Brontë · written 1846, published 1850 · Whole poem, 28 lines

No coward soul is mine,
No trembler in the world’s storm-troubled sphere:
I see Heaven’s glories shine,
And faith shines equal, arming me from fear.

O God within my breast,
Almighty, ever-present Deity!
Life—that in me has rest,
As I—undying Life—have power in Thee!

Vain are the thousand creeds
That move men’s hearts: unutterably vain;
Worthless as withered weeds,
Or idle froth amid the boundless main,

To waken doubt in one
Holding so fast by Thine infinity;
So surely anchored on
The stedfast rock of immortality.

With wide-embracing love
Thy spirit animates eternal years,
Pervades and broods above,
Changes, sustains, dissolves, creates, and rears.

Though earth and man were gone,
And suns and universes ceased to be,
And Thou were left alone,
Every existence would exist in Thee.

There is not room for Death,
Nor atom that his might could render void:
Thou—Thou art Being and Breath,
And what Thou art may never be destroyed.

POEM 4 · EMILY BRONTË (WRITTEN 1846, PUBLISHED 1850)
5
“Dover Beach”
Matthew Arnold · 1867 · Whole poem, 37 lines; or the continuous span from “The sea of faith” to the end (23 lines)

The sea is calm to-night.
The tide is full, the moon lies fair
Upon the straits; on the French coast, the light
Gleams and is gone; the cliffs of England stand,
Glimmering and vast, out in the tranquil bay.
Come to the window, sweet is the night-air!
Only, from the long line of spray
Where the sea meets the moon-blanched sand,
Listen! you hear the grating roar
Of pebbles which the waves draw back, and fling,
At their return, up the high strand,
Begin and cease, and then again begin,
With tremulous cadence slow, and bring
The eternal note of sadness in.

Sophocles long ago
Heard it on the Ægean, and it brought
Into his mind the turbid ebb and flow
Of human misery: we
Find also in the sound a thought,
Hearing it by this distant northern sea.

The sea of faith
Was once, too, at the full, and round earth’s shore
Lay like the folds of a bright girdle furled.
But now I only hear
Its melancholy, long, withdrawing roar,
Retreating, to the breath
Of the night-wind, down the vast edges drear
And naked shingles of the world.

Ah, love, let us be true
To one another! for the world, which seems
To lie before us like a land of dreams,
So various, so beautiful, so new,
Hath really neither joy, nor love, nor light,
Nor certitude, nor peace, nor help for pain;
And we are here as on a darkling plain
Swept with confused alarms of struggle and flight,
Where ignorant armies clash by night.

POEM 5 · MATTHEW ARNOLD (1867)
6
“Invictus”
William Ernest Henley · written 1875, published 1888 · Whole poem, 16 lines

Out of the night that covers me,
Black as the Pit from pole to pole,
I thank whatever gods may be
For my unconquerable soul.

In the fell clutch of circumstance
I have not winced nor cried aloud.
Under the bludgeonings of chance
My head is bloody, but unbowed.

Beyond this place of wrath and tears
Looms but the Horror of the shade,
And yet the menace of the years
Finds, and shall find, me unafraid.

It matters not how strait the gate,
How charged with punishments the scroll,
I am the master of my fate:
I am the captain of my soul.

POEM 6 · WILLIAM ERNEST HENLEY (WRITTEN 1875, PUBLISHED 1888)
7
“Ulysses,” the closing lines
Alfred Tennyson · 1842 · The continuous span from “There lies the port” to the last line, 27 lines. The whole poem is 70 lines.

There lies the port: the vessel puffs her sail:
There gloom the dark broad seas. My mariners,
Souls that have toil’d, and wrought, and thought with me—
That ever with a frolic welcome took
The thunder and the sunshine, and opposed
Free hearts, free foreheads—you and I are old;
Old age hath yet his honour and his toil;
Death closes all: but something ere the end,
Some work of noble note, may yet be done,
Not unbecoming men that strove with Gods.
The lights begin to twinkle from the rocks:
The long day wanes: the slow moon climbs: the deep
Moans round with many voices. Come, my friends,
’Tis not too late to seek a newer world.
Push off, and sitting well in order smite
The sounding furrows; for my purpose holds
To sail beyond the sunset, and the baths
Of all the western stars, until I die.
It may be that the gulfs will wash us down:
It may be we shall touch the Happy Isles,
And see the great Achilles, whom we knew.
Tho’ much is taken, much abides; and tho’
We are not now that strength which in old days
Moved earth and heaven, that which we are, we are;
One equal temper of heroic hearts,
Made weak by time and fate, but strong in will
To strive, to seek, to find, and not to yield.

POEM 7 · ALFRED TENNYSON (1842)
Record and submit
 
Option A: record
Record yourself, eyes covered, on any device; a phone is fine. Upload the file or paste a link, named LastName_FirstName_Recitation_M3_ELA11. Add a caption or short transcript: the exact lines you recited, with the title and, for poems 1 and 2, the chapter.
Option B: live
Your teacher may instead schedule a live recitation with you, also with eyes closed. If so, they will tell you, and you do not submit a video.
How this is scored
 
CriterionStrongDeveloping
7
Accuracy of text
points		From memory, eyes covered, faithful to the words and the line order; slips are rare and self-recovered.Frequent errors, skipped stanzas, or long stalls; or eyes open / clearly reading.
7
Vocal delivery
points		Clear and controlled; pace, pause, and stress follow the sense, not just the line ends; the meter is felt without being pounded.Rushed or flat; a sing-song beat that ignores meaning; pauses only at line breaks; hard to follow.
6
Interpretation
points		Delivery choices show real understanding of the poem's turn and its weight.Recited correctly but with little sense of what the words mean or where the poem turns.
Total: 20 points.

assignments.title: Quarterly Reading Check: Module 3
assignments.html:
Quarterly Reading Check: Module 3
English 3 · Module 3 · Independent Reading
20 pointsRecord / Upload MediaAbout 3 minutesDue in Week 8
The book
 
›One book of choice per quarter, from the Optima Independent Reading library.
›Not a book the class reads this year. No book used twice, in any quarter or year.
›A title not on the list is subject to teacher approval.
Open the Optima Independent Reading library ↗
Record one of four, equal weight
 
1
Oral Book Response
about 3 minutes
Answer these five out loud, in order. Notes in front of you are fine; a script read word for word is not.
1What is the book, and how far did you get?
2Pick one character. What do they want, and what is in the way?
3Describe a moment where that character makes a choice you would not have made. Why did they make it?
4Read one sentence or short passage you marked, and say why that one.
5Who should read this book, and who should skip it?
2
Dramatic Reading
about 3 minutes
1Choose a passage of roughly 150 to 300 words where a character is under pressure: deciding, arguing, afraid, or hiding something.
2Read it aloud as that character. Decide before you record what they want in this moment, then let your pace, volume and pauses show it.
3Then talk for about a minute: who is this character, what do they want here, and what did you do with your voice to show it? Name one specific choice you made.
3
Make the Case
about 3 minutes
You are a guest on a books podcast and the host has given you three minutes to make one argument. House rule of the show: you have to take the side most listeners will not.
1Name what you are arguing about, and say where it falls in the book. Pick something people genuinely disagree over: a moral dilemma, a turn nobody saw coming, or a decision a character made that readers still argue about.
2Take the unpopular side and say it in your first sentence. If most readers think the character was right, argue that they were wrong. If nobody could disagree with your claim, it is not an argument yet.
3Give two pieces of evidence from the text: a line, a scene, something a character says or does. Say roughly where each one falls.
4Answer the strongest objection, the one the host would come back at you with. State it fairly first, then answer it.
5Land it. Finish with one sentence a listener would still be turning over after the episode ends.
4
A Different Ending
about 3 minutes
Only take this one if you finished the book. You are going to replace the ending, and you cannot rewrite an ending you never got to.
1Say how the book actually ends, in two or three sentences. Be accurate. The rest of this only works if your listener knows what you are changing.
2Name the exact point where your version branches off, then describe your ending in detail. What happens, who it happens to, and how does it finish?
3Explain why yours is better for this book. Not happier, and not kinder to your favourite character, but truer to what the story has been about. Name the idea or theme you are serving.
4Say what your ending costs. Every ending gives something up. Name what is lost by not keeping the one the author wrote.
What your teacher listens for
 
Where you are
Give a page, a chapter, or “about two thirds through.”
Something exact
Read or quote one short line.
Something yours
A judgement, a disagreement, a question.
One moment
One scene closely beats the whole story vaguely.
How far you got
“I stopped at chapter nine because ___” earns more than a confident account of an ending you never reached.
A clear voice
You can be heard the whole way through.
A note on AI tools
 
A summary tool can tell you what happens in a book. It cannot tell you which page you stopped on, which line you read twice, or what you thought was wrong. Those are the things these options ask for.
Delivery
 
›Record / Upload Media records into Canvas, or upload an audio or video file. Say the title and author in your first sentence.
›Audio only is complete. Video is permitted, never required.
›Two attempts. The later one is graded.
How this is scored
 
CriterionFull creditPartialNone
7
Evidence of actual reading
points		Specific details only a reader would know: a named moment, a line, where it falls in the book.Accurate but general enough to have come from a summary.No evidence of having read it.
7
Insight beyond summary
points		Explains a character's motive or makes a claim about the book, in the student's own words, and points at something specific.Names a character or a claim but retells plot instead of explaining it.Plot summary only, or not addressed.
6
Oral delivery
points		Clear, audible, well paced; speaks to the listener; not read off a script.Understandable but flat or script-bound.Cannot be understood.
Total: 20 points.

discussions.title: Module 3 Forum: Why Does Jane Refuse to Remain with Rochester?
discussions.html:
Module 3 Forum: Why Does Jane Refuse to Remain with Rochester?
English 3 · Module 3
10 pointsGraded discussionOne post, one replyDue in Week 5
In chapter 27, Rochester offers Jane every argument he has: his suffering, his years of loneliness, the unfairness of a law that binds him to a marriage that was never a real union in any way that matters to him. Jane's own feelings argue his case for him, loudly, from inside her own mind. And still she leaves before dawn, on foot, with twenty shillings, saying to herself, "I care for myself. The more solitary, the more friendless, the more unsustained I am, the more I will respect myself."
Post and reply
 
1Post (by mid-week): Take a position: does Jane make the right choice in refusing to stay with Rochester, or does her principle cost more than it is worth? In four to six sentences, defend or challenge her choice with one quotation from chapter 27, cited by chapter. Name specifically what she gains and what she loses by leaving.
2Reply (by end of week): Respond to a classmate who took a different position from yours. Point to one line in the text that complicates their reading, and ask one honest question about it.
Guidance
 
›Argue from what the text actually shows Jane paying and gaining, not from a general opinion about the situation. Chapter 27 gives you both sides of the argument in her own words; use them.
›Defending her choice and questioning whether it was worth the cost are not opposite positions. You can agree she was right and still name what it cost her.
›If you introduce Jane or Rochester by name in your post, define who they are at this exact point in the novel with an appositive, not a summary sentence.
How this is scored

Full
points		Clear position, one cited quotation from chapter 27, names both what is gained and what is lostEngages a different position with a specific line and a real question

discussions.title: The Thornfield Chronicle: Pitch Your Feature
discussions.html:
The Thornfield Chronicle: Pitch Your Feature
English 3 · Module 3
10 pointsGraded discussionOne post, two repliesDue in Week 8
Pitch the angle for your informative feature on one part of Jane's world, written for a general reader.
Post
 
Post (by the end of Week 8), your pitch, in 4 to 6 sentences:
1Which angle are you writing: (a) the real position of a Victorian governess, (b) the Gothic mode and why Brontë uses it, (c) inheritance, marriage law, and money in the novel, or (d) the shape of a coming-of-age story and how Jane Eyre fits and bends it?
2What is the lead sentence you plan to open with, the one that has to hook a stranger in the first line?
3Who is your "general reader," specifically? (Not "everyone." A magazine subscriber who has never read the novel, a student researching Victorian England, a modern reader curious about the period: pick one and say so.)
4What does that reader most need explained before the rest of your feature makes sense?
5Name one source you expect to use (a text, a database, or a specific search you plan to run in JStor).
Reply
 
Reply (by the start of Week 9) to at least TWO classmates. For each reply, name one specific thing that makes the angle clear to a stranger who has never read the novel, and ask one honest question, a place the lead might confuse a new reader, a fact that seems to need a source, or an angle that might be broader than 900 to 1,200 words can hold.
Guidance
 
›A strong lead hooks a stranger, not a classmate who already knows the novel.
›Useful feedback is specific: "Your lead assumes the reader already knows what a governess's salary tells you about her social rank. One sentence naming that rank before you compare it would fix it" is.
›Every submission stays a solo piece; this discussion only trades feedback.
›This discussion opens in Week 8 and stays open through the start of Week 9.
How this is scored
